steps.scope_of_what_this_proves: A digest-bound exhibit list DETECTS an altered exhibit. It does not AUTHENTICATE it: the list is unkeyed, so a party who can rewrite both the exhibit and the list can re-seal both. findings.title: A default-config fresh clone of this repository cannot be recovered at an ordinary path on this host, and the remediation is recorded nowhere in the repository
findings.measurement: R1: git clone at a 127-character destination exits 128 with 'unable to checkout working tree'; the resulting repository reports all 940 tracked paths as staged deletions. R2: the same command at a 24-character destination exits 0 with all 940 files present. R3: the same 127-character destination succeeds when core.longpaths=true is supplied on the command line.
findings.root_cause: The longest tracked path is 169 characters. Windows MAX_PATH is 260 including the terminating NUL, so the usable path is 259 and the maximum destination is 89 characters (measured, see step R2). core.longpaths=true is set in this working copy's LOCAL git config only (global and system are UNSET), and R3.8 measures that a fresh clone does NOT inherit it -- core.longpaths is UNSET inside the recovered clone.
findings.consequence: The one setting that makes this repository recoverable lives in .git/config, which is the exact artifact a disaster destroys. An operator recovering from history alone has no way to learn it from the repository, and the naive command fails in a way that still leaves a directory that looks like a clone.
findings.relation_to_prior_evidence: Extends A3-700 finding F1 (sealed verification fails under a long Windows path) and shares a root cause with A4-800 open defect D1 (mission_store.py:81-92 writes receipts through a longer temporary filename with no long-path handling).
findings.what_would_fix_it: Any of: shorten the longest tracked path enough that ordinary destinations fit (the current 169 leaves only 89 characters); document `git -c core.longpaths=true clone` in the repository where a recovering operator will find it; or ship a bootstrap that sets core.longpaths in a fresh clone. None is in this node's write scope.

findings.title: A first, non-retained run of this exercise reported a transient inconsistent working tree
findings.measurement: In a first run at 2026-08-13T05:04:45Z, a successful core.longpaths clone made into a directory that had just been rm -rf'd (the failed R1 clone) reported 16 porcelain status lines immediately afterwards, and a subsequent checkout printed 'D' lines for long paths. The retained run avoided reusing any destination directory and reported 0 porcelain lines; two clean re-probes also reported 0.
findings.status: NOT REPRODUCED and NOT EXPLAINED. The most likely cause is Windows deletion latency on the just-removed directory tree, but that is a hypothesis, not a measurement.
findings.why_recorded: It was observed. Dropping an observation because it did not reproduce is how a readiness record becomes decoration.

what_this_exercise_did_not_do: No production system, deployment target, external storage, or paid service was contacted.
No external append-only retention was exercised. G4 and B-GOV-04 are closed and no such adapter exists; the production retention claim belongs to those gate rows, not to this exercise.
No incident-response path was exercised -- no paging, rotation, on-call, or containment drill. No such system exists in this repository, and B-OPS-04 owns the production claim.
Recovery was from a LOCAL clone on the SAME host. Durability against loss of this host is not demonstrated; that is precisely B-GOV-04's exit condition.
The recovered artifact was verified against a digest recorded in the same repository. That is self-consistency, not independent attestation (see R5 scope).
